clinicalPearls: Unilateral, mottled blue-grey to brown pigmentation in the distribution of the ophthalmic (V1) and maxillary (V2) divisions of the trigeminal nerve
Frequently involves the sclera, conjunctiva and other ocular structures (oculodermal melanocytosis), and ipsilateral glaucoma can develop, so ophthalmology review is important
More common in individuals of Asian and African descent and in females; it may be present at birth or first appear around puberty
The pigment is dermal, so it is not accentuated by Wood lamp and topical lightening agents are ineffective
Pigment-specific Q-switched or picosecond lasers are the treatment of choice for the cutaneous component
Rarely, melanoma may arise within cutaneous, uveal or leptomeningeal melanocytes, so new nodules or visual change require prompt assessment
Bilateral involvement is uncommon but recognised and warrants consideration of associated conditions
reference.pathophysiology: During embryogenesis melanocytes derived from the neural crest normally migrate to the epidermis, but in naevus of Ota some are arrested within the dermis. These entrapped, melanin-producing dermal melanocytes scatter light to give a characteristic blue-grey (Tyndall) hue, and their distribution follows the ophthalmic and maxillary trigeminal branches. The same melanocytic population can involve ocular tissues, accounting for scleral pigmentation and the associated glaucoma and, rarely, melanoma risk.
additionalInvestigations: Ophthalmic examination with intraocular pressure and glaucoma screening
Dermoscopy to characterise the dermal pigment pattern
Serial photography to monitor for change
Biopsy of any nodular or clinically suspicious area to exclude melanoma
Neuroimaging if leptomeningeal melanosis or neurological features are suspected
redFlags: A new nodule, thickening or focal change suggesting cutaneous or uveal melanoma
Rising intraocular pressure or visual disturbance indicating glaucoma
Neurological symptoms raising concern for leptomeningeal melanocytosis
Rapid extension or ulceration of the pigmented area
reference.prognosis: The naevus is benign and persists lifelong if untreated, with good cosmetic improvement achievable using pigment-specific lasers; the main long-term concerns are glaucoma and a small risk of ocular or cutaneous melanoma.
pitfalls: Overlooking the need for ophthalmic review and glaucoma screening
Attempting to treat the dermal pigment with topical lightening agents
Missing an evolving melanoma within the lesion or eye
Confusing it with a Mongolian spot or acquired melasma
management: Reassure that the lesion is benign and treat the cutaneous component for cosmetic reasons with pigment-specific Q-switched or picosecond lasers, as topical lightening agents are ineffective on dermal pigment
Arrange ophthalmology review with intraocular pressure measurement and glaucoma screening for oculodermal melanocytosis
Undertake long-term surveillance for melanoma arising in cutaneous, uveal or leptomeningeal melanocytes, assessing new nodules or visual change promptly
Monitor with serial photography for change
Biopsy any nodular or clinically suspicious area to exclude melanoma
Arrange neuroimaging if leptomeningeal melanosis or neurological features are suspected
